pr.title: Let a stack carry several projects, with a header for each
pr.head: cea9ed6a6feef51320d45bef339653d3d9c961fd

summary: Projector's site lists the pull requests that have summaries on its Reviews index, and each summary page has a sidebar that lists the pull requests of its stack, the chain of pull requests built on each other. The stack-header plan, merged in #216 and not yet built, gives each stack a header above its rows: the project it carries out, linked to that project's page, or a short title when it has none. A project here is a plan under docs/projects/.

That plan allowed one header per stack. A stack can carry more than one project, though: one layer finishes a plan and the next starts another. With one header, the build had to show one project, hide the others, and print a warning on every such stack.
This pull request amends the plan before it is built. It changes one Markdown file and no code:

• Each pull request still records one project or none. No single pull request names several.
  • The build splits each stack into segments. A segment is a run of consecutive layers that carry the same project, and each segment gets its own header. A layer with no project joins a neighboring segment instead of heading one.
  • The stack stays one group. The Reviews index and the sidebar keep the stack in one place, in GitHub's order, with a header above each segment.
  • The warning goes. Layers that name different projects are now normal.

The new § 8 holds the whole design: the segment rule, the segments data both pages read, the markup with worked examples, the rejected options, and acceptance tests. The earlier sections now point at § 8 where they used to describe one header per stack. The plan stays at status: ready, which claims it can be built as written.

cards.title: Terms on this page
cards.html:
• Stack: pull requests built on each other, bottom layer first. The build reads stacks from GitHub's stacks API, or from base branches when GitHub has none.
  • Layer, member: one pull request in a stack.
  • Group: the members of a stack that have a summary on the site, which are the rows the Reviews index can show.
  • Segment: a run of consecutive layers that carry one project, with its own header.
  • Header: a project's title linked to its page, or a plain title for a stack with no project.

cards.title: What the reviews settled
cards.html:
The first review asked for changes with two findings, both places where the plan specified one behavior two ways. This head fixes both, and the second review is clean:

  • Where a layer with no project lands. It joins the segment of the member before it in the stack's order. In a stack with a branch, that member can sit on another branch. § 8.5 adds a row for this case.
  • What stack_segments takes. It takes every member of the stack, members without a summary included, rather than only the group. A title header with no name takes the title of the first member with a summary.

The head also merges main, which changes no other file in this pull request.

groups.title: Segments replace one header per stack
groups.kicker: The stack-header plan, amended to give each run of same-project layers its own header
intro: The plan file is the whole change. Read the new § 8 first: it states the rule, then the data, then what the reader sees, then why, then the tests. The edits to §§ 1 to 4 replace each mention of one header per stack with a pointer to § 8, and keep every section number they cite.

stack_segments, a new function in the site build, walks every member of the stack bottom first, in the order find_stacks gives, members without a summary included. The first segment starts at the bottom and takes the first project any member names. A later member that names a different project starts a new segment. A member that names the same project, or none, joins the current one, which is the segment of the member before it. In a stack with a branch, that member can sit on another branch. A stack where no member names a project is one segment under a title.

Each summary page's data gains segments, a list of {header, members}, which the sidebar draws with a new stackSegmentsHtml. Each row of the index's site.json carries its own segment's header. The index starts a new table body wherever a row's header differs from the one above it in the same stack. When the Open or Closed box hides a whole segment, the segments on either side join when they name the same project.

checks.text: The index claims hold against current code. showReviews in site/src/site.ts calls reviewsTable(shown) again on every box change, so the index can compare the rows it actually draws. The divider the plan turns off for a continued body is the tbody tr:last-child td border in site/assets/site.css.
At this head, project check reports the plans valid, the unit suite passes with 543 tests and 1 skipped, and the Testing section's 80-column awk check prints only the two lines it names.

files.note: The plan. The new § 8 holds the segment design, and §§ 1 to 4 point at it.

checks.text: The heading still says "one project or a title", although the plan now draws a header for each project. The site shows this heading as the project's title, and the JSON examples quote it. The review lists retitling as a suggestion.

This row now agrees with § 8.1. A member with no project sits under the segment of the member before it in the stack's order. I checked § 2.1, § 8.1, and the new § 8.5 row for #15, which is based on #9's branch, and all three give #15 alpha/beta's segment.

stack_segments now takes every member from find_stacks here, in § 2.6, and in § 8.2. That matches § 8.1 and the § 8.5 row that expects #11, which has no summary, in alpha's segment. No sentence still says it takes the group.

The prose says a list in a stack of several segments is labeled with its header's title, but the markup below it uses Pull requests for and the title. Read the two as the same label. The review suggests making the wording match.
